subject: stat_density Produces Incorrect Kernel Density Estimates

messages.author: 7b36a5521b8eb4d4
messages.subject: stat_density Produces Incorrect Kernel Density Estimates
parts:
Consider an example that has two groups. One has twice as much data as the other, but the values are the same.

plotData <- data.frame(expr = c(rep(c(5, 10), each = 5), rep(c(5, 10), each = 10)), groups = rep(c("Poor", "Good"), c(10, 20)))
ggplot(plotData, aes(x = expr, colour = groups)) + stat_density(aes(y = ..density..), geom = "path", size = 1, adjust = 0.5) + scale_colour_manual("Vital", values = c("red", "blue")) + theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(), axis.line = element_blank()) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 16))

The area under both curves is not the same.

messages.author: 373beb702917b8b5
messages.subject: Re: stat_density Produces Incorrect Kernel Density Estimates
parts:
The area under the curves are in fact the same, but those areas are
stacked on top of one another. This makes sense for the default
geom_area, but not for geom_path; when using the path geom you should
also change the position adjustment, e.g.,

ggplot(plotData,
aes(x = expr, colour = groups)) +
stat_density(aes(y = ..density..), geom = "path", size = 1, adjust = 0.5) +

scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 16))

or take the easy way ant use geom_density() instead of stat_density():

ggplot(plotData,
aes(x = expr, color = groups)) +
geom_density(adjust=0.5) +
scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 16))


Best,
Ista

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: stat_density Produces Incorrect Kernel Density Estimates
parts:
Hi:

If you maintain everything else in your code and add position =
"identity" to the stat_density() call, you'll get the same answer as
Ista's. By default, position = "stack" in stat_density(), which
produces the effect that Ista described re area plots - position
"identity" plots the density estimates as is in each group. Even
though the peaks are different in each group, the areas under the
curves are the same - this is visible by noting that the tails of the
'Good' distribution are shorter than those from the 'Poor' one.

Dennis
